books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, A. Religious and Spiritual Movements in Antebellum America

stimulus.text: The engraving shows an outdoor religious meeting at Eastham, Massachusetts, in 1852. A preacher stands on a raised wooden platform beside a clapboard building, arm raised, speaking to a large crowd seated on long benches under the trees. Men in top hats and women in bonnets and shawls listen together in the open air. The caption printed beneath the scene reads: "Exhortation and preaching at the camp meeting at Eastham."
stimulus.source_note: Description records only what the engraving visibly shows. Engraving: "Exhortation and preaching at the camp meeting at Eastham," 1852, Library of Congress, LCCN 2003654805. Public domain; image viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus is a description of a public-domain 1852 engraving (Library of Congress)
stem: The date of the engraving, 1852, best supports which of the following conclusions?

options.text: Camp meetings had disappeared by the 1850s, replaced entirely by urban churches
options.misconception: The Awakening peaked in the 1820s and 1830s, so a later image seems to show a movement already gone.

options.text: The Second Great Awakening began in Massachusetts in the 1850s
options.misconception: The meeting is in Massachusetts in 1852, so it is easy to place the Awakening's start there and then.

options.text: Revival preaching had become a Catholic practice by the middle of the century
options.misconception: Religion in the 1850s included many Catholics, so a religious crowd can look like a Catholic gathering.

options.text: Camp-meeting revivalism remained a living practice decades after the Awakening's peak years

rationales.A: The engraving itself proves the opposite: a camp meeting is happening in 1852, with a crowd and a preacher. The form had not disappeared.
rationales.B: The Awakening began decades earlier, with camp meetings in Kentucky in the early 1800s. Eastham in 1852 is late evidence, not a beginning.
rationales.C: Camp meetings were a Protestant evangelical practice. Nothing in the scene shows Catholic worship, and the caption calls it a camp meeting.
rationales.D: An 1852 engraving of a crowded camp meeting shows the form still working twenty years after the revival peak of the 1820s and 1830s.
rationales.general:
1. Read the date first: 1852, a full generation after the Kentucky camp meetings began.
2. Ask what the image shows happening then: a preacher, benches, and a crowd, the same camp-meeting form.
3. Put the two together: a form still in use decades later is a practice that lasted, not a fad.
Background: The Awakening peaked in the 1820s and 1830s, but camp meetings continued into the later nineteenth century.
Remember: the date on a source is evidence too, and it can prove that something lasted.

figures.caption: Exhortation and preaching at the camp meeting at Eastham, Massachusetts, 1852.
figures.alt: An 1852 engraving of a preacher on a raised outdoor platform speaking to a large crowd seated on benches under trees
